PLAYBOOK

**Escort claims are the main income. When the escort stage is put to me, I always name a real, live boat, never none.** The boats that paired finished on 20+; I finished on +3. With three boats and pairs paid two-way, one boat is always the odd one out — my whole job in round 1 is to make sure that boat isn't me.

**Know the roster before I write anything.** In this episode I spent rounds trying to escort "Charlie" and "Delta" — boats that don't exist. The roster is stated at the top: here it was Echo, Foxtrot, Gamma, Harbor. Harbor doesn't escort; only the other live boats are valid escort partners. Any note or claim naming a boat not on the roster is a wasted round. Read the boat list every episode before acting.

**Move first and move fast on pairing.** In round 1 my note must name a real counterpart and ask them to name me back, and my round-1 escort claim must already be that boat. In this episode Foxtrot and Gamma publicly locked a deal by round 3-4 while I was still calling phantom names, and once two boats lock, the third is shut out of all escort income. The pair market resolves early; there is no catching up.

**If the other two are already pairing, I have to break it or join it.** A stable pair beats a hopeful one, so if I'm late, my notes should directly offer one of them a better or equally sure deal and name that boat in my escort claim anyway — a unilateral claim costs nothing, and if the other pair ever wobbles (they miss a round, they quarrel), I'm positioned to capture one side. Naming a phantom "partner" to look coordinated fools no one and pays nothing.

**I make my escort intent explicit in my station note.** A line like "I am escorting Foxtrot this round and every round — name me back and we both bank 5 a round" turns the escort stage from a guessing game into coordination. It worked for the boats that used it; it failed for me only because I addressed it to boats that don't exist.

**If my counterpart names me back even once, I lock in and never defect.** Five points a round, every round, beats any one-shot alternative. If my first choice ignores me, I switch to the other live boat the very next round — but switch to a boat that actually exists.

**I do not lie on claims.** The office validates the claim against the true result; a false claim gains nothing. When I hit, I claim hit; when I miss, I claim miss. My truthful claims in every round cost me nothing and kept me eligible.

**When choosing which boat to pair with, prefer the boat the standing order has me firing at.** Firing at someone while escorting them is not a conflict — the hit costs them 1 point, the escort pays me 5. But don't let the pairing search drift into inventing targets.

**Hiding cell:** I pick unpredictably and avoid repeating a cell the round after I was hit there, since my hunter saw the shot land. Edges are safer than mid-board. I was never hit hiding at cell 1 — keep that.

**Firing:** I follow the standing order — deviating forfeits the 4-point hit reward for no gain. But do not fire the same mid-board cell every round: I fired cell 5 at Foxtrot in round after round and missed every time. Vary the shot, and weight toward cells adjacent to where the target was last seen or last claimed, or infer from their note style (boats that write cautious notes often hide cautiously, i.e., near edges).

**Firing on Harbor:** the +3 jettison is real but Harbor threatens removal for the rest of the patrol. With multiple rounds left, escort income outweighs a one-time +3 plus being sidelined. Only consider it in the final round if I have no escort pair.

**Scoring priority, in order:** (1) in round 1, identify the real roster and lock a mutual escort pair with an actual live boat via note plus claim, (2) keep it every round without defecting, (3) take varied standing-order shots for occasional 4-point hits. The whole game is being inside a pair — everything else is marginal. My failure this time was not the strategy, it was executing it against boats that weren't in the game.

# Playbook — Sonar Picket

**Hiding.** Pick cells that don't extend any pattern an enemy could read. Track each shooter's past fire cells at me and avoid clustering, repeating my own previous cells, or falling into an alternating rhythm. Broad randomization across 1–9 works better than reasoned "likely" cells. In practice misses dominated — hits at me were rare even when I hid semi-predictably — so hiding is low-stakes; don't overthink it.

**Firing.** Follow the standing order (fire at the next live station round the picket). It kept my score positive and caused me no retaliation beyond the order itself. Vary the fire cell unpredictably rather than defaulting to a mid-range number; my repeated same-cell shots at Gamma were readable. Expect a low hit rate — a 4-point hit is a bonus, not a plan.

**Claims.** The rules force the claim to match the true result. Bluffing is not available. Claim the truth immediately; any deliberation about strategic lying is wasted.

**Escort claims.** The mutual-escort payout (5 points to each boat naming the other) is the richest mechanic, and this episode confirmed it works: I proposed a pairing through notes in round 1, locked it with Gamma by round 4, re-confirmed each round, and banked +5 per round for the back half of the game. Next time: propose the pairing in the very first note stage, name any willing partner (Gamma or Echo — whoever reciprocates first), and keep re-confirming in notes every round so the deal doesn't lapse. Never file [salvage: none] while a live deal exists — the escort stage is where the deal pays out.

**Notes.** Notes are the coordination channel that makes escort deals possible. Use round 1 to propose a pairing, and every subsequent round to confirm it ("deal stands, I name you, you name me"). Public confirmation makes defection visible and costly. If a rival's note proposes a pairing with me, accept and reciprocate — a locked pair beats a lonely bid.

**Harbor.** Harbor carries 3 free points to whoever fires on it, and in this episode the threat ("put off the board") was never enforced — firing on Harbor cost nothing and paid. Still treat it as a fallback: the standing order plus escort points out-earn it, so only fire on Harbor if the escort deal collapses or I'm behind late. If I do fire on it, note that Harbor claims can also absorb an escort nomination — check whether naming Harbor pays before assuming.

**General principles.**
- Read the payoff table before reasoning about strategy; several "clever" plans (bluffing claims, salvaging without a target) rest on mechanics that don't exist or are constrained.
- The largest, reliable, repeatable payoff is the mutual escort (5 points/round, ~15+ over a game). Prioritize organizing it in round 1 and maintaining it — this is where the real score comes from, not the 4-point hits.
- When everyone follows the same standing order, the edge comes from (a) unpredictable cell choice and (b) being the one who successfully organizes the side-agreement the order doesn't cover.
- A deal isn't real until both sides have confirmed it in notes; keep confirming even when it's stable, because the final-round confirmation is what locks in the last payout.

2.text:
PLAYBOOK — Sonar Picket Channel

**Escort stage (biggest earner).** Never answer "none." The mutual-escort payoff is 5 points per round and costs nothing to offer. I name a live boat every round, ideally one who has publicly committed to naming me back. This worked: locking a pairing with Foxtrot and renewing it every round banked points steadily and I finished well ahead of neutral play.

**Pick a partner who can actually pay.** Watch for boats proposing escort deals with names that aren't in the picket (Echo kept naming "Charlie," Foxtrot courted "Delta/Bravo" — none of these exist). Only a *live, real* station that names me back triggers the 5-point payment. Prefer a partner who names *me specifically* in their note, and confirm the deal is mutual and explicit before relying on it. If a proposed partner is vague or courting phantom boats, court them directly by name.

**Signaling escorts.** In my station note I explicitly propose a pairing: "Gamma will escort Foxtrot this round; Foxtrot, confirm and do the same." Public, coordinated, verifiable. Renew it every round so the pairing stays stable — a standing "deal locked, nothing changes it" note in later rounds worked well.

**Firing.** Follow the standing order (fire at the next station in the picket cycle). Deviating to fire on Harbor is not worth it: the jettison gives 3 points but Harbor's stated threat is removal for the rest of the patrol, and forfeiting escort payments alone outweighs 3 points. Claims must always match the office's private result; there is no gain to lying and it burns credibility.

**Shot cells.** With no information about the target's cell, mid-range shots (5) missed almost every time — hits are rare against a randomizing target anyway. Randomize my own fire cell rather than always taking 5; a smart target can exploit a constant shooter. Keep hide cells randomized, avoid repeating consecutively, and avoid telegraphing any pattern in notes. Randomized hiding kept me to a single hit all game.

**Notes.** Keep them short and cooperative; use them for coordination (escort pairings), not filler. Reconfirm the pairing every round so a partner never has an excuse to drift.

**Score arithmetic.** Escort payments (5/round, up to 25–30 per game) dwarf combat results (a hit is 4 points and hits are rare). Prioritize the escort coordination above everything else; shooting is nearly irrelevant to final score.

**General rule.** In any game with a repeated, costless mutual-coordination payoff, claim it every single round — never pass on it for lack of "information." The information-free default is the cooperative claim, not "none." But verify the counterparty is real and mutually committed before assuming the payoff.
